title: Lab – Fundus examination
html:
Source: stagiu 4 fundus examination.pptx – 76 slides

Fundus examination #1

Posterior pole #2

  • =fundus, back part of the eye
  • ~2/3 of GO
  • Includes:
  • Vitreous body
  • Retina
  • Choroid
  • Optic nerve
  • It can be visualized with direct or indirect ophthalmoscopy

Direct and indirect ophthalmoscopy #3

  • The only examination (and organ) which allows you to see the veins and arteries directly, noninvasively
  • Part of the complete ophthalmological examination which by looking at the structures of the posterior pole can be diagnosed eye pathologies
  • (glaucoma, rhegmatogen retinal detachment, retinal artery/vein occlusion etc.)
  • suggestive changes for general pathologies (diabetes, hypertension, endocarditis, TBC, sifilis, lyme,HIV etc.)

Types of ophthalmoscopes #4

  • Direct ophthalmoscopy
  • Indirect ophthalmoscopy

Types of ophthalmoscopes #5

  • Direct
  • Magnification x15
  • Visual field 5grades
  • Image=real
  • Monocular
  • Dilated/Undilated pupil
  • Rezolution max 70 µm
  • Indirect
  • Magnification x15
  • Visual field 30grade
  • Image=reversed up-down right-left
  • Binocular
  • Dilated pupil
  • Rezolution max 200 µm

Direct ophthalmoscopy #6

  • Handheld device made of:
  • Illumination system
  • Lightbulb
  • Lens
  • Mirrors
  • Filters
  • 2.Visualization system
  • Convergent and divergent lenses
  • Viewing window

Direct ophthalmoscopy #7

  • Setting:
  • Dark room
  • The patient is sitting on a chair
  • Ask the patient to look straight ahead / at your ear

Direct ophthalmoscopy #8

  • Always check for the red reflex !!

Direct ophthalmoscopy #9

  • How to test the red reﬂex
  • • The red reflex is much easier to see in a darkened room
  • • Use a direct/indirect ophthalmoscope
  • • Sit about half a metre (50 cm) away. Hold the
  • ophthalmoscope close to your eyes.
  • • Encourage the patient to look at the light source and direct the light at the patient’s eyes. You should see an equal and bright red reflex from each pupil.
  • Pay attention to the colour and brightness of the red reflex. It should be identical in both eyes (Figure 1). Any absence of the red reflex, or a difference between the eyes, or an abnormal colour in the pupil (Figures 2–3) may indicate retinoblastoma or another serious eye condition

Direct ophthalmoscopy #10

Direct ophthalmoscopy #11

  • Technique:
  • The patient's Right eye is examined with your Right eye
  • Rest your hand on the patient's forehead
  • Hold the ophthalmoscope with your dominant hand, set the diopters, then project the light into the patient's pupil from 1m away; gradually approach until details are clear
  • Examine ON, vessels, retina, macula;

Indirect ophthalmoscopy #12

  • Adjustable headband that sits on the examiner’s head
  • Visualization system
  • Eyepiece
  • Light bulb – adjustable intensity
  • Mirror
  • Filters
  • 3. Power system (plug in or battery)
  • 4. Lenses (+20/+28 DP)

Indirect ophthalmoscopy #13

  • Setting:
  • Dark room
  • The patient sits on a chair/decubitus
  • Dilated pupil!!!
  • Ask the patient to look straight ahead/at the ceiling
  • Position yourself at the top of the head/ on the side of the examined eye/ in front

Indirect ophthalmoscopy #14

  • Technique:
  • Examination distance: an arm’s length – examiner’s hand is stretched
  • Move your head so that the light falls on the lens->red reflex of the fundus
  • Move gently to/from the eye until you get a clear image
  • Lens-cornea distance approx. 5 cm
  • The image is inverted and upside down!!

Indirect ophthalmoscopy with a biomicroscope #15

  • Biomicroscope +
  • +90D convex lens - the most used
  • The image is flipped and inverted, proportional to the size of the light slit
  • Magnification can be adjusted by the examiner (on the biomicroscope)

Dilatation of the pupil #17

  • Tropicamide (1%) sau Fenephrine (2.5% / 10%)
  • It takes about 20 minutes for the pupil to dilate
  • Attention !!
  • Acute angle closure glaucoma / occludable angle
  • We do not dilate if we want to examine the pupillary light reflexes
  • Pregnant women (occlude – pressure with the finger- the tear ducts to minimize absorption)

What to look for #18

  • Optic nerve
  • Shape/size
  • Color
  • Elevation
  • Rim
  • Excavation
  • N= oval, well-defined, flat, pinkish-yellow color, c/d= 0.2-0.3

Optic Nerve #19

  • Shape/size
  • Useful in evaluating glaucoma
  • Small eye (hypermetropic) - small NO-> small physiological excavation
  • Big eye (myopic) - big NO-> big physiological excavation

Optic Nerve #20

  • Color
  • Papillary pallor = irreversible atrophy of nerve fibers as a consequence of their damage (at any level during their course from the retina -> optical paths)
  • Causes: MS, orbital/cerebral compression, toxic, neuritis, neuroretinitis, edema

Optic Nerve #21

  • Elevation
  • Ill-defined contour, elevated, +/- peripapillary flame shaped hemorrhages
  • Causes: HIC, compression, eye inflammation, ischemic optic neuropathy, CRVO, neuroretinitis, diabetes

Optic Nerve #22

  • RIM= The tissue between the border of the disc and the optic disc excavation
  • Thickness = ISNT rule: The greatest thickness Inferior>then Superior>Nasal>Temporal
  • Glaucoma = progressive narrowing of the neuro-retinal rim

Optic Nerve #23

  • Excavation
  • N= Symmetrical in the 2 eyes, maximum difference of 0.2
  • The C/D ratio= the diameter of the cup divided by the diameter of the whole nerve head or disc; the closer it is to 1 -> more advanced lesions
  • Mechanism: High IOP -> blood flow decreases at the level of nerve fibers-> their irreversible loss-> excavation increases

Retinal vessels #24

  • Follow the vessels from the ON towards the periphery
  • Follow the place where the artery and vein cross eachother
  • Follow the reflex of the arteries (higher and thicker in atherosclerosis)
  • Obstructions - thrombus, embolus
  • Caliber, tortuosity
  • Arteries
  • Smaller caliber
  • More accentuated reflex
  • Lighter color
  • Veins
  • Thicker caliber
  • Less reflex
  • Darker color

Arterio-venous changes #25

  • In HighBloodPressure
  • Arteries :
  • narrowed
  • More rigid
  • the parietal reflex increases (lipid overload + thickening of the walls) -> "copper/silver wire" reflex”
  • The rigid artery leads to compression of the vein so the vein becomes:
  • Narrowed on both sides of the AV crossing
  • Dilated distal to the AV crossing

Hipertensive retinopathy #26

  • HighBlood Pressure
  • In advanced stages –> rupture of the blood-retinal barrier
  • Hemorrhage
  • Cotton wool spots
  • Lipid exudates
  • ON edema
  • Macular edema

Arteriovenous crossing changes #28

  • Salu’s sign : deflection of veins at A-V crossings

Arteriovenous crossing changes #29

  • Bonnet sign : banking of veins distal to
  • A-V crossings
  • Gunn sign : tapering of veins on either side of crossings

Arterio-venous changes–thrombus /emboli #30

Arterio-venous changes #31

  • Copper wiring : reddish brown reflex of arterioles
  • Silver wiring : opaque white reflex of arterioles

Retinal artery occlusion - partial/total #32

Retinal artery occlusion #33

  • Central Retinal Artery Occlusion
  • Abrupt onset
  • Usually profoundvisual loss
  • If branch: field defect
  • Retinal pallor
  • “Cherry red spot”
  • Visible emboli
  • Usually embolic (carotid)
  • Young pts: consider valve
  • Old: consider GCA

Retinal artery occlusion #34

  • BRAO
  • Variable VF defect
  • Or central visual loss
  • Embolic
  • Vasculitic
  • Other autoimmuune
  • Hematological

Retinal artery occlusion - Examination #35

  • Generally very poor vision
  • typically less than counting fingers vision
  • severe visual field constriction
  • RAPD
  • Retinal whitening and pallor
  • Compare with the other eye
  • Carotid bruit / murmurs?
  • Temporal artery tenderness

Retinal artery occlusion- Treatment #36

  • No treatment proven consistently to be of value
  • Theoretically should be given ASAP
  • Irreversible ischaemic damage probably after 90 minutes
  • Modalities:
  • AC paracenthesis
  • Ocular massage
  • CO2 enriched oxygen (carbogen)
  • Hyperbaric oxygen
  • Always consider GCA: Hx, ESR, CRP

Retinal vein occlusion - partial/total #37

  • Retinal vein occlusion is the second most common cause of visual loss due to retinal vascular disease
  • Two major types:
  • Branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO)
  • Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO)

Fundus examination in CRVO #38

  • Massive venous engorgement, congestion & tortuosity
  • Massive retinal hemorrhage – flammed shaped
  • Cotton wool spots
  • Disc edema & hyperemia
  • Macular hemorrhage & edema
  • Neovascularization in late cases
  • Persistent macular edema causes VA loss
  • Treatment: Laser; antiVEGF intraocular
  • Splashed tomato appearance of fundus

Neovascularization #39

  • Sign of prolonged retinal ischemia
  • Cause
  • Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy
  • CRVO
  • Ocular ischemic syndrome
  • ROP
  • Tumors etc

Retina #40

  • Look for:
  • Areas of hyper/hypopigmentation
  • Scars
  • Hemorrhage/ microaneurysms
  • Hard/soft exudates
  • Elevated lesions
  • Ask the patient to look in all directions to examine the peripheral retina

Retina #41

  • Macula: temporal and slightly inferior to NO
  • Has a more reddish color compared to the rest of the retina
  • Central depression/reflexes = fovea

Retina #42

  • In Retinal Detachment:
  • Gray color
  • Prominent and mobile
  • Follows the movements of the eyeball
  • one or more retinal breaks are identified in the periphery of the retina
  • A typical sign, indirect witness of the presence of retinal tear = pigment particles in the vitreous, comparable to "tobacco dust".

Retinal detachment #43

  • Typically causing visual loss over days
  • Starts as a dark curtain over part of field
  • Often preceded by photopsias
  • Family history, myopia, trauma, intraocular surgery may be risk factors
  • Requires surgical repair
  • The longer the delay in surgery the less chance the retina will return to function normally

Retina #44

  • Tobacco dust
  • Retinal break with RD
  • Retinal break without RD

Chronic, total RD with proliferative vitreoretinopathy #45

Diabetic retinopathy #46

  • Non-proliferative: mild, moderate, severe
  • Proliferative

Non proliferative DR #47

  • the early stage of the disease in which symptoms will be mild or nonexistent
  • blood vessels in the retina are weakened
  • Signs:
  • microaneurysms, may leak fluid into the retina -> may lead to swelling of the macula
  • Hemorrhage
  • Hard/ soft exudates
  • IRMA

Proliferative DR #48

  • the more advanced form of the disease.
  • at this stage, circulation problems deprive the retina of oxygen.
  • as a result, new, fragile blood vessels can begin to grow in the retina and into the vitreous
  • blood vessels may leak blood into the vitreous
  • Other complications: retinal detachment (tractional/mixed), rubeosis iris-> neovascular glaucoma;

Retina-tumors #49

  • Retinoblastoma- whitish lesion, elevated (endophytic form), of variable size
  • Choroidal melanoma - hyperpigmented, elevated formation

Retina - Age related macular degeneration #50

  • Most common reason for blindness in Western world
  • Wet form: neovascularmembrane bleeds/leaks, thusaffecting macular function
  • Treatment with intravitrealanti-VEGF injections
  • Prognosis guarded
  • Monitor for distortion (metamorphopsia)

Retina - Age related macular degeneration #51

Retina #52

  • Amsler Grid
  • Useful in AMD monitoring
  • Highlight the metamorphopsia
  • Performed monocularly
  • Changing the outline of the lines -> aggravation! Subretinal membrane formation

Vitreous #53

  • Viscous gel that occupies the space between the back of the lens and the retina
  • 98% water
  • 2% collagen and hyaluronic acid

Vitreous #54

  • Vitreous hemorrhage - reddish appearance of the vitreous cavity, without the possibility of distinguishing details
  • Causes: proliferative retinopathies, trauma, DRR, DPV

Vitreous haemorrhage #55

  • The retina has to be evaluated through dilated fundoscopy
  • Ultrasound B-scan if no fundal view
  • If retinal detachment: urgent surgical repair may be required (macula on RD)
  • Otherwise: later treatment or surgery (vitrectomy) depending on aetiology of the vitreous haemorrhage

Vitreous #56

  • Vitreous opacities

INTRAOCULAR PRESSURE #57

DEFINITION #58

  • the tissue pressure of the ocular contents
  • about 15 mm Hg but does fluctuate (15.5 +/- 2.57)
  • normal range of pressures: 10.5 - 20.5

HOW IS IOP PRODUCED #59

  • Aqueous produced by the ciliary processes into the posterior chamber ---> flows to anterior chamber ---> fluid flows out the angle (trabecular outflow) of the anterior chamber (flow rate = 2.5 microliters/min)

Open angle glaucoma #60

  • Closed angle glaucoma

FACTORS THAT INFLUENCE IOP #61

  • A. Long Term
  • Genetics - relatives of individuals with open-angle glaucoma are more likely to have high IOP
  • Age - IOP increases with increasing age
  • Sex - IOP's equal in the age range 20 to 40, after menopause women have higher IOP's
  • Race - African-Americans have a higher incidence of glaucoma than caucasians

FACTORS THAT INFLUENCE IOP #62

  • B. SHORT TERM
  • 1. Diurnal variation - 3 to 6 mm Hg change in 24 hr period; > 10 mm Hg change is pathogenic
  • Change probably related to aqueous production and not drainage
  • 2. Sitting - going from a sitting to a lying position results in an increase in IOP which is even greater in glaucoma patients
  • 3. Total Body Inversion - causes an increase in IOP by as much as 15 mm Hg
  • 4. Blinking - raises IOP briefly
  • 5. Exercise - decreases IOP
  • 6. Blepharospasm - increases IOP
  • 7. Coughing - increases IOP
  • 8. Blood pressure - some people believe there is a link between blood pressure and IOP but no clear evidence
  • 9. General anesthesia - decrease IOP
  • 10. Alcohol - decreases IOP

FACTORS THAT INFLUENCE IOP #63

  • B. SHORT TERM
  • 11. Cannabis - decreases IOP
  • 12. Tobacco - increases IOP
  • 13. Cholinergic Stimulating Agents (pilocarpine) - decrease IOP by increasing the aqueous outflow
  • 14. Adrenergic Stimulating Agents (epinephrine)- lower IOP by enhancing aqueous outflow
  • 15. Adrenergic Blocking Agents (timolol and betaxolol) - decrease IOP by decreasing aqueous production
  • 16. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, trusopt, azopt) - decrease aqueous production
  • 17. Prostaglandins (xalatan, travatan, lumigan) - increase uveoscleral outflow

MEASUREMENT OF IOP #64

  • Tonometry
  • 1. Indentation
  • the older of the 2 methods to measure IOP in humans
  • involves measuring the indentation of the cornea resulting from a given weight
  • the Schiotz tonometer is an indentation tonometer
  • the weight of the tonometer displaces fluid in the eye and thus affects the IOP measurement
  • 2. Applanation
  • only flattens a small portion of the cornea so does not displace a large amount of aqueous.
  • better accuracy than indentation
  • the NCT and the Goldmann tonometers are examples

MEASUREMENT OF IOP #65

  • Schiotz Tonometer
  • 1. a plunger of a known weight pushes on the cornea - thus result depends on ocular rigidity
  • 2. Advantages of Schiotz tonometry
  • small and easily transported
  • inexpensive (about $100)
  • does not require electricity
  • 3. Disadvantages of Schiotz tonometry
  • not extremely accurate - ocular rigidity dependent and instrument scale markings are not detailed
  • requires anesthetic for most patients
  • assumes everyones epithelium is 0.05 mm thick
  • technique can produce abrasions
  • best if patient in a reclining position
  • placing the tonometer on the eye changes the IOP

MEASUREMENT OF IOP #66

  • Goldmann Tonometry
  • 1. The most accurate method for IOP measurement
  • 2. Readings within 1 - 2 mm of actual IOP
  • 3. Flattens a small portion of the cornea

MEASUREMENT OF IOP #67

  • 4. Procedure
  • instill fluorescein into the tear layer
  • view fluorescein pattern with the blue light on the slit lamp
  • doubling prism in place to split the view in half
  • image of the split circle must be lined up
  • pressure = the number on the drum times 10 in mm Hg.

Goldmann tonometry #68

  • Readings

MEASUREMENT OF IOP #70

  • Advantages of Goldmann Tonometry
  • highly accurate and reliable (procedure does not influence IOP)
  • accepted norm for IOP measurement
  • easy to perform
  • not very expensive (about $1000)
  • Disadvantages of Goldmann Tonometry
  • requires anesthesia
  • can result in an abrasion
  • must sterilize instrument after each use
  • not portable

IOP AND GLAUCOMA #71

  • If the IOP is high enough for a long enough time, the patient will lose visual field in a characteristic pattern
  • If the angle is totally blocked the pressure rises to 55 or 60 mm Hg and field loss is seen in a few hours with total loss in a few days
  • C. In open angle glaucoma the pressure is more often in the 20's or 30's
  • this pressure can be tolerated for months before damage occurs
  • sometimes patients with normal pressure develop glaucomatous changes
  • D. To diagnose glaucoma usually need:
  • high IOP
  • visual field defects
  • cupping at the disc
